units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Arithmetic and geometric sequences
units.caps: CAPS Grade 12 Mathematics, Term 1: Number patterns, sequences and series (arithmetic and geometric sequences; general term; sum of series; sigma notation)
units.intention: Today I am finding the general term of arithmetic and geometric sequences.
units.prompt: How do you tell if a sequence is arithmetic or geometric?

lesson.say: An arithmetic sequence adds the same number each time, called the common difference, d. The general term is T n equals a plus n minus one, times d.
lesson.html:
3, 7, 11, 15 …→d = 4→Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d

a is the first term.

lesson.say: A geometric sequence multiplies by the same number each time, called the common ratio, r. The general term is T n equals a times r to the power n minus one.
lesson.html: 2, 6, 18, 54 …→r = 3→Tₙ = a·rⁿ⁻¹

lesson.say: Here is the sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic series. It is n over two, times two a plus n minus one d. For a geometric series it is a times r to the n minus one, over r minus one.
lesson.html:
Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]→Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1)

These are on the formula sheet.

example.q: Find the 20th term of 5, 8, 11, 14 …
steps: Arithmetic: a = 5, d = 3.

questions.q: Is 4, 12, 36, 108 … arithmetic or geometric?
questions.explain: The ratio is constant (3), so it is geometric.

questions.q: Find T₁₀ for 2, 7, 12, 17 …
questions.explain: T₁₀ = 47.

questions.q: Find T₆ for 3, 6, 12, 24 …
Find the sum of the first 10 terms of 1, 3, 5, 7 …
What is the common difference of 20, 16, 12, 8 …?

options: Writing out a, d or r

units.parent: Your child worked with arithmetic and geometric sequences and series.
units.teacher: Shows identifying sequence type, finding general terms and calculating sums of series.
units.done: Arithmetic adds a constant difference; geometric multiplies by a constant ratio.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Introduction to differentiation
units.caps: CAPS Grade 12 Mathematics, Term 2: Differential calculus (average gradient; derivative from first principles; rules of differentiation; equation of a tangent; cubic graphs; optimisation)
units.intention: Today I am finding derivatives and understanding what they mean.
units.prompt: What does a derivative tell you about a graph?

lesson.say: The derivative tells you the gradient of a curve at any point, which is the instantaneous rate of change. For a straight line the gradient is constant. For a curve it changes.
lesson.html:
Gradient of a curve→=→rate of change

Written f′(x) or dy/dx.

lesson.say: To differentiate x to the n, multiply by n and reduce the power by one. The derivative of x cubed is three x squared. The derivative of a constant is zero.
lesson.html: d/dx (xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹→d/dx (x³) = 3x²→d/dx (5) = 0

lesson.say: At a turning point, the gradient is zero. So set the derivative equal to zero to find maximum and minimum points. This is used in optimisation.
lesson.html:
f′(x) = 0→→→turning point

Businesses use this to find maximum profit or minimum cost.

example.q: Find f′(x) if f(x) = 4x³ − 2x² + 7.
steps: 4x³ → 12x².

questions.q: Differentiate: f(x) = x⁵
questions.explain: f′(x) = 5x⁴.

questions.q: Differentiate: f(x) = 3x² + 6x
What is the derivative of a constant, like 9?
questions.explain: The derivative of a constant is 0.

questions.q: f(x) = x² − 4x. At what x-value is the turning point?
What does f′(x) represent?
options: The gradient of f at x
questions.explain: f′(x) is the gradient of the curve at x.

units.parent: Your child started differential calculus: finding derivatives and turning points.
units.teacher: Shows interpreting the derivative as gradient, applying the power rule and finding turning points.
units.done: The derivative gives the gradient. Set it to zero to find turning points.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Loans and savings plans
units.caps: CAPS Grade 12 Mathematics, Term 1: Finance, growth and decay (future value and present value annuities; loans and bond repayments; sinking funds)
units.intention: Today I am understanding how regular payments build savings and repay loans.
units.prompt: Why does a longer loan cost more in total?

lesson.say: If you save the same amount regularly, interest makes it grow. The future value formula is F equals x times one plus i to the n, minus one, all over i.
lesson.html:
F = x[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1] / i

x = regular payment, i = interest rate per period, n = number of payments.

lesson.say: A loan's present value is how much you borrow today. The formula is P equals x times one minus one plus i to the minus n, all over i. You solve it to find the monthly payment x.
lesson.html:
P = x[1 − (1 + i)⁻ⁿ] / i

Home loans, called bonds, work this way.

lesson.say: The longer the loan, the more interest you pay in total, even if each payment is smaller. Compare the total paid, not only the monthly instalment.
lesson.html:
Total paid = x × n

Interest rate per month = annual rate ÷ 12.

example.q: You repay R3 000 a month for 60 months. How much do you pay in total?
steps: Total = payment × number of payments.

questions.q: Which formula is for saving regular amounts?
questions.explain: Regular savings use the future value annuity formula.

questions.q: An annual interest rate of 12% compounded monthly. What is i per month?
R2 500 per month for 72 months. Total paid?
Why does a 30-year bond cost more in total than a 20-year bond for the same house?
questions.explain: Interest accumulates over more years.

questions.q: What is the present value of a loan?
questions.explain: It is the amount borrowed now.

units.parent: Your child learned how regular savings grow and how loan repayments work.
units.teacher: Shows distinguishing future and present value annuities, converting rates and evaluating total loan cost.
units.done: Future value builds savings; present value works out loan payments. Always compare the total cost.

units.subject: Mathematical Literacy
units.title: VAT, payslips and income tax
units.caps: CAPS Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy: Finance (VAT; payslips and deductions; income tax using tax brackets and rebates)
units.intention: Today I am working out VAT, net pay and income tax.
units.prompt: What would you like to know about your first payslip?

lesson.say: Value-added tax, or VAT, is added to most goods and services. This lesson uses South Africa's rate of 15 percent. To add VAT, multiply by 1.15. To find the price before VAT, divide by 1.15.
lesson.html:
Before VAT × 1,15→= price with VAT

Price with VAT ÷ 1,15 = price before VAT

lesson.say: A payslip shows gross pay, which is what you earn, then deductions such as PAYE income tax, UIF and pension. What you take home is the net pay. Workers pay 1 percent of their pay to UIF.
lesson.html: Gross pay→− deductions→= net pay

lesson.say: Income tax uses brackets: higher incomes are taxed at higher rates. You work out the tax on taxable income, then subtract a rebate. SARS publishes new tables every year, so always use the current ones.
lesson.html: This lesson uses a made-up, simplified tax table for practice, not SARS's real one.

example.q: Practice table: tax = 18% of taxable income, minus a rebate of R17 000. Annual taxable income is R150 000. What is the tax for the year?
steps: Subtract the rebate: 27 000 − 17 000 = R10 000.
Tax for the year: R10 000, about R833 a month.

questions.q: A kettle costs R300 before VAT. What does it cost with 15% VAT, in rand?
A price including 15% VAT is R230. What was the price before VAT, in rand?
Gross pay is R9 000. Deductions are R1 350. What is the net pay, in rand?
UIF is 1% of gross pay. Gross pay is R9 000. What is the UIF deduction, in rand?
Practice table: tax is 18% of taxable income, minus a R17 000 rebate. Someone earns R80 000 a year, and 18% of R80 000 is R14 400. How much tax do they pay?
options: R0, because the rebate is more than the tax
questions.explain: The rebate is bigger than the tax, so they pay no income tax.

units.parent: Your child calculated VAT, read a payslip and used a practice tax table.
units.teacher: Shows calculating VAT-inclusive and VAT-exclusive amounts, interpreting payslip deductions, and applying tax brackets and rebates (practice table).
units.done: VAT: × 1,15 or ÷ 1,15. Net pay = gross pay − deductions.

units.subject: Mathematical Literacy
units.title: Packing and packaging
units.caps: CAPS Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy: Measurement (surface area and volume of rectangular prisms and cylinders; packing problems; cost of materials)
units.intention: Today I am working out surface area, packing and material costs.
units.prompt: Why do you think some boxes have so much empty space?

lesson.say: Surface area is the total area of all the faces of an object. Think of the cardboard needed to make a box. A box has six rectangular faces in three matching pairs.
lesson.html: Surface area of a box = 2(l × b) + 2(l × h) + 2(b × h)

lesson.say: How many small boxes fit in a big box? Divide each length of the big box by the matching length of the small box. Round each answer down to whole boxes. Then multiply the three answers.
lesson.html: Length ÷→Width ÷→Height ÷→Round down, then multiply

lesson.say: Once you know the surface area, multiply by the price per square metre to find the cost of material. Add extra for overlaps and waste.
lesson.html: Packers and builders often add about 10% for waste.

example.q: Boxes of 10 cm × 10 cm × 10 cm are packed into a crate 50 cm × 30 cm × 20 cm. How many fit?
steps: 50 ÷ 10 = 5 along the length.
30 ÷ 10 = 3 across, and 20 ÷ 10 = 2 high.

questions.q: Find the surface area of a box 10 cm × 5 cm × 2 cm, in cm².
Small boxes are 20 cm × 20 cm × 20 cm. A crate is 100 cm × 60 cm × 40 cm. How many boxes fit?
A crate is 45 cm long. Boxes are 10 cm long. How many fit along the length?
hints: You can't fit half a box.
questions.explain: 4,5 rounds down to 4 whole boxes.

questions.q: A box needs 2 m² of cardboard. Cardboard costs R12 per m². What does the cardboard cost, in rand?
Which job needs surface area rather than volume?
questions.explain: Wrapping paper covers the outside: surface area.

units.parent: Your child worked out surface area, packing and material costs.
units.teacher: Shows calculating surface area, solving packing problems with whole objects, and costing materials.
units.done: Outside: surface area. Inside: volume. Pack in whole boxes only.

units.subject: Mathematical Literacy
units.title: Building from plans
units.caps: CAPS Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy: Maps, plans and other representations (floor plans and elevation plans; scale drawings; calculating quantities of building materials)
units.intention: Today I am using building plans to work out the materials needed.
units.prompt: What would you need to build a room?

lesson.say: A floor plan shows a building from above. An elevation shows it from the front, back or side, so you can see heights, doors and windows.
lesson.html: Floor plan: from above→Elevation: from the side

lesson.say: Builders use plans to work out how much material is needed. For a wall, first find its area. Subtract the area of the windows and doors. Then multiply by the number of bricks that cover one square metre.
lesson.html: Wall area→− windows and doors→× bricks per m²

lesson.say: You can't buy part of a bag of cement. When ordering materials, always round up to whole units.
lesson.html: 23,2 bags means you buy 24 bags.

example.q: A wall is 5 m long and 2,4 m high, with a 1 m² window. About 50 bricks cover 1 m². How many bricks are needed?
steps: Wall area: 5 × 2,4 = 12 m².
Subtract the window: 12 − 1 = 11 m².

questions.q: Which drawing shows how high a house's windows are?
hints: Height is seen from the side.
questions.explain: Elevations show the building from the side, with heights.

questions.q: A wall is 4 m by 2,5 m. What is its area, in m²?
A wall of 10 m² has a door of 2 m². About 50 bricks cover 1 m². How many bricks are needed?
questions.explain: 8 m² × 50 = 400 bricks.

questions.q: You need 13,4 bags of cement. How many bags must you buy?
hints: You can't buy part of a bag.
questions.explain: Round up to 14 whole bags.

questions.q: Scale 1 : 50. A window is 3 cm wide on the elevation. How wide is it really, in metres?

units.parent: Your child read building plans and worked out the materials needed.
units.teacher: Shows distinguishing plan and elevation views, calculating areas less openings, applying scale, and rounding quantities up in context.
units.done: Find the area, take away the openings, and always round materials up.

units.subject: Mathematical Literacy
units.title: Comparing data sets
units.caps: CAPS Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy: Data handling (quartiles and box-and-whisker plots; comparing two data sets; evaluating claims made with data)
units.intention: Today I am comparing two sets of data and checking claims.
units.prompt: What makes you believe or doubt a statistic in the news?

lesson.say: Order the data. The median splits it in half. The lower quartile is the middle of the lower half. The upper quartile is the middle of the upper half.
lesson.html:
Minimum→Q1→Median→Q3→Maximum

Interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 − Q1

lesson.say: A box-and-whisker plot draws the five-number summary. The box shows the middle half of the data. Comparing two boxes shows which group is higher, and which is more spread out.
lesson.html: A longer box means more spread in the middle half.

lesson.say: When someone uses data to make a claim, ask three questions. How big was the sample? Who was asked? Does the average hide a big spread?
lesson.html: Ask: who was asked, how many, and how spread out?

example.q: Class A test marks: Q1 = 45, median = 60, Q3 = 70. Class B: Q1 = 55, median = 62, Q3 = 66. Compare them.
steps: The medians are close: 60 and 62.
Class A's IQR is 70 − 45 = 25. Class B's is 66 − 55 = 11.
Similar averages, but Class B's marks are much more consistent.

questions.q: Find the median of 3, 7, 8, 12, 15, 18, 20.
hints: The data is in order, with 7 values.
questions.explain: The 4th of 7 values is 12.

questions.q: Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 35. What is the interquartile range?
Two taxi routes have the same median trip time. Route A's IQR is 5 minutes and Route B's is 20 minutes. Which route is more reliable?
questions.explain: Route A's times vary less, so it is more reliable.

questions.q: A shop says 9 out of 10 customers prefer its bread, after asking 10 people in its own shop. What is the main problem?
options: The sample is small, and only includes its own customers
9 out of 10 is too high to be real
questions.explain: 10 of its own customers is a small, biased sample.

questions.q: On a box-and-whisker plot, what does the box show?
options: The middle half of the data
hints: The box goes from Q1 to Q3.
questions.explain: The box spans Q1 to Q3, the middle half.

units.parent: Your child compared two sets of data using quartiles, and checked claims made with data.
units.teacher: Shows calculating quartiles and IQR, interpreting box-and-whisker plots to compare data sets, and critiquing sampling behind claims.
units.done: Compare the centre and the spread, and ask who was asked and how many.

units.subject: Mathematical Literacy
units.title: Fair games and expected results
units.caps: CAPS Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy: Probability (theoretical and experimental probability; fairness of games; risk and expected outcomes in lotteries and insurance)
units.intention: Today I am judging whether games are fair, and what to expect over many plays.
units.prompt: Why do you think lotteries make money?

lesson.say: Theoretical probability is what should happen, like a half for heads. Experimental probability is what actually happened in trials. With more trials, the results usually get closer to the theory.
lesson.html: 10 tosses: 7 heads→1 000 tosses: about 500 heads

lesson.say: A game is fair if every player has the same chance of winning. For example, player A wins on a 1 or 2. Player B wins on a 3, 4, 5 or 6. Then player B is twice as likely to win.
lesson.html:
A: 2/6→B: 4/6

Not fair: B is twice as likely to win.

lesson.say: Expected winnings are the average result over many plays: the chance of winning times the prize. Compare that with what you pay. Lotteries are designed so that players lose money on average.
lesson.html: A R5 ticket with a 1 in 1 000 chance of winning R2 000: expected winnings are R2 a ticket, so on average you lose R3.

example.q: A spinner has 4 equal parts. 1 part wins R10, and 3 parts win nothing. It costs R3 to play. Is it worth playing?
steps: Chance of winning: 1/4.
Expected winnings: 1/4 × R10 = R2,50.
You pay R3, so on average you lose 50c a game.

questions.q: A coin is tossed 10 times and lands heads 7 times. What does this show?
options: Small experiments can differ from the theory
Heads has a 70% chance for ever
questions.explain: In a few trials, results often differ from the theory.

questions.q: A wins if a dice shows 1, 2 or 3. B wins on 4, 5 or 6. Is the game fair?
options: No, A is more likely to win
No, B is more likely to win
questions.explain: Each player has 3 of the 6 numbers: 1/2 each.

questions.q: A R10 ticket has a 1 in 100 chance of winning R500. What are the expected winnings per ticket, in rand?
The same ticket costs R10, and the expected winnings are R5. What happens on average?
hints: Compare what you pay with what you expect to win.
questions.explain: You pay R10 and get back R5 on average: a R5 loss.

questions.q: Which is a fair game for two players with one dice?
options: Each player wins on 3 of the 6 numbers
Player B wins only on a 6
Player A wins on 1 and 2, and B on 6
questions.explain: Only the first gives both players the same chance.

units.parent: Your child tested whether games are fair, and saw why lotteries lose money on average.
units.teacher: Shows distinguishing theoretical and experimental probability, judging fairness, and calculating expected value in context.
units.done: Fair means equal chances. Expected winnings = chance × prize.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Novel extract: The Year of Small Rains
units.caps: CAPS Grade 12 English Home Language: Literature (novel: characterisation, symbolism, setting, theme; contextual questions and literary essay)
units.intention: Today I am analysing character, symbolism and theme in a novel extract.
units.prompt: What do you think Nosipho should choose?
units.passage:
From: The Year of Small Rains (a 2to.iQ novel extract)

The letter from the university arrived on the same day the borehole dried up. Nosipho held it in one hand and the empty bucket in the other, and for a moment she could not decide which mattered more.

Her grandmother was sitting on the stoep, shelling peas into a chipped enamel bowl. She did not look up. "So," she said. "You are leaving us."

"I haven't even opened it, Makhulu."

"You don't need to. I can see it in your shoulders." The old woman split another pod with her thumbnail. "Your mother had the same shoulders. Like a bird before it flies."

Nosipho put the bucket down. Somewhere beyond the dry fields, a hadeda cried out, harsh and certain. She tore open the envelope.

lesson.say: Read the extract, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
From: The Year of Small Rains (a 2to.iQ novel extract)

The letter from the university arrived on the same day the borehole dried up. Nosipho held it in one hand and the empty bucket in the other, and for a moment she could not decide which mattered more.

Her grandmother was sitting on the stoep, shelling peas into a chipped enamel bowl. She did not look up. "So," she said. "You are leaving us."

"I haven't even opened it, Makhulu."

"You don't need to. I can see it in your shoulders." The old woman split another pod with her thumbnail. "Your mother had the same shoulders. Like a bird before it flies."

Nosipho put the bucket down. Somewhere beyond the dry fields, a hadeda cried out, harsh and certain. She tore open the envelope.

lesson.say: A symbol is an object that stands for an idea. The letter represents opportunity and the future. The empty bucket and dried borehole represent hardship and the needs of home.
lesson.html:
Letter: the future→Empty bucket: hardship at home→Bird: freedom, leaving

Holding both shows Nosipho's conflict.

lesson.say: Makhulu does not look up, which suggests she is hiding her feelings. Her comparison to a bird before it flies shows she understands and accepts that Nosipho will leave. Themes include sacrifice, family, and the pull between home and ambition.
lesson.html: Sacrifice→Family→Home vs ambition

example.q: What is the effect of the borehole drying up on the same day the letter arrives?
steps: The two events happen together.
Opportunity arrives just as home needs her most.
It sharpens Nosipho's dilemma and creates tension.

questions.q: What does the empty bucket symbolise?
options: Hardship and the needs of home
questions.explain: It represents hardship and the needs of home.

questions.q: Why does Makhulu not look up?
options: She may be hiding her emotions
She is angry at the peas
hints: She is facing a painful moment.
questions.explain: Not looking up suggests she is hiding her feelings.

questions.q: Like a bird before it flies is an example of …
questions.explain: It uses like, so it is a simile.

questions.q: Which theme is most clearly shown?
questions.explain: The extract explores home versus ambition.

questions.q: What does a hadeda cried out, harsh and certain suggest about Nosipho's decision?
options: It mirrors a firm, perhaps painful, decision
hints: Right before she opens the letter.
questions.explain: The harsh, certain cry mirrors her decision.

reflect.q: How did you analyse the extract?

units.parent: Your child analysed a novel extract for character, symbolism and theme.
units.teacher: Shows interpreting symbolism, indirect characterisation, figurative language and theme.
units.done: Symbols, characters and setting work together to build a theme.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Exam comprehension skills
units.caps: CAPS Grade 12 English Home Language: Reading and Viewing (comprehension: literal, inferential, evaluative and appreciative questions; quoting; own words)
units.intention: Today I am learning how to answer different types of comprehension questions.
units.prompt: Which type of question do you find hardest?

lesson.say: Literal questions ask for facts found in the text. Inferential questions ask you to read between the lines. Evaluative questions ask for your judgement, with reasons.
lesson.html: Literal: find it→Inferential: work it out→Evaluative: judge it

lesson.say: Look at the key word in the question. Quote means copy exact words in quotation marks. In your own words means do not copy. Explain means give a reason.
lesson.html:
Quote→Own words→Explain→Discuss

Check the mark allocation: 2 marks usually needs 2 points.

lesson.say: Answer in full sentences. Do not repeat the question. For evaluative questions, say whether you agree or not, then justify with evidence from the text.
lesson.html: Answer→Evidence→Reason

example.q: Question: Explain what Makhulu means by I can see it in your shoulders. (2 marks)
steps: Explain needs a reason. 2 marks needs two points.
Point 1: Makhulu reads Nosipho's body language.
Point 2: Nosipho's posture shows she is ready and eager to leave.

questions.q: What type of question is: Where was Makhulu sitting?
hints: Is the answer directly in the text?
questions.explain: The answer is stated directly.

questions.q: Quote a phrase that shows the setting is dry. What should you do?
options: Copy exact words in quotation marks
Write it in your own words
questions.explain: Quote exact words from the text in quotation marks.

questions.q: A question is worth 3 marks. How many points should you make?
questions.explain: Usually about one point per mark.

questions.q: Do you think Makhulu is a sympathetic character? What type of question is this?
questions.explain: It asks for your judgement with reasons.

questions.q: Which is the best way to start an answer?
options: Answer directly in a full sentence
questions.explain: Answer directly in a clear sentence.

reflect.q: What will you do in the exam?

units.parent: Your child practised answering literal, inferential and evaluative comprehension questions.
units.teacher: Shows distinguishing question levels, responding to instruction words and using mark allocation.
units.done: Read the instruction word, check the marks, and support answers with evidence.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Formal speech and interviews
units.caps: CAPS Grade 12 English Home Language: Listening and Speaking (prepared formal speech; interview skills; body language; register)
units.intention: Today I am preparing for a formal speech and a job or university interview.
units.prompt: What makes a speaker confident?

lesson.say: A good speech starts with something that gets the audience's attention. This is called a hook. Then it gives three clear points with examples. It ends strongly, so the audience remembers it.
lesson.html:
Hook→Point 1→Point 2→Point 3→Memorable ending

Use cue cards with keywords, not full sentences.

lesson.say: Make eye contact, vary your pace and tone, pause for effect, stand still and use natural gestures. Practise out loud, not just in your head.
lesson.html:
Eye contact→Pace→Pauses→Posture

Nerves are normal. Breathe slowly before you start.

lesson.say: Research the organisation. Prepare answers to common questions, like tell me about yourself. Use examples from your life. Prepare a question to ask them at the end.
lesson.html:
Research→Prepare examples→Dress appropriately→Ask a question

Use the STAR method: Situation, Task, Action, Result.

example.q: Interview question: Tell me about a time you solved a problem. How could you answer using STAR?
steps: Situation and task: our school garden had no water during the drought.
Action: I organised learners to collect grey water.
Result: the garden survived and fed the school's nutrition programme.

questions.q: What is a hook in a speech?
questions.explain: A hook grabs the audience's attention.

questions.q: What should cue cards contain?
options: The full speech word for word
questions.explain: Keywords remind you what to say, so you do not need to read it all.

questions.q: What does STAR stand for?
questions.explain: Situation, Task, Action, Result.

questions.q: Which is good delivery?
questions.explain: Eye contact and pauses improve delivery.

questions.q: Why prepare a question for the interviewer?
questions.explain: It shows genuine interest and preparation.

units.parent: Your child learned how to structure and deliver a speech and prepare for interviews.
units.teacher: Shows speech structure, delivery techniques and interview preparation using STAR.
units.done: Hook your audience, deliver with confidence, and use STAR in interviews.

units.subject: Life Sciences
units.title: DNA and protein synthesis
units.caps: CAPS Grade 12 Life Sciences, Term 1: DNA, the code of life (structure of DNA and RNA; DNA replication; protein synthesis: transcription and translation; DNA profiling)
units.intention: Today I am learning how DNA carries instructions to make proteins.
units.prompt: Why does a change in DNA sometimes change a protein?

lesson.say: DNA is a double helix, like a twisted ladder. The sides are sugar and phosphate. The rungs are pairs of bases: adenine pairs with thymine, and guanine pairs with cytosine.
lesson.html:
A–T→G–C

The order of bases is the genetic code.

lesson.say: In transcription, a section of DNA, a gene, is copied into messenger RNA in the nucleus. RNA uses uracil instead of thymine.
lesson.html:
DNA→→ transcription →→mRNA

In RNA, A pairs with U.

lesson.say: In translation, the mRNA moves to a ribosome. Every three bases, called a codon, code for one amino acid. Transfer RNA brings the amino acids, which join to form a protein.
lesson.html: mRNA codons→→ ribosome →→protein

example.q: A DNA strand reads TAC GGA. What is the mRNA?
steps: Pair each base: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C.
TAC → AUG. GGA → CCU.
mRNA: AUG CCU.

questions.q: In DNA, adenine pairs with …
questions.explain: A pairs with T in DNA.

questions.q: Where does transcription happen?
questions.explain: Transcription happens in the nucleus.

questions.q: Which base replaces thymine in RNA?
questions.explain: RNA uses uracil.

questions.q: What is a codon?
options: Three bases that code for one amino acid
questions.explain: A codon is three bases coding for one amino acid.

questions.q: Put protein synthesis in order.
items: Amino acids join into a protein
questions.explain: Transcription, move to ribosome, tRNA brings amino acids, protein forms.

units.parent: Your child learned how DNA is copied into RNA and used to make proteins.
units.teacher: Shows DNA structure, base pairing, transcription and translation.
units.done: DNA is transcribed to mRNA, which is translated into protein.

units.subject: Life Sciences
units.title: Genetics and inheritance
units.caps: CAPS Grade 12 Life Sciences, Term 2: Genetics and inheritance (genes, alleles, genotype, phenotype; dominance; monohybrid crosses; Punnett squares; blood groups)
units.intention: Today I am using Punnett squares to predict inheritance.
units.prompt: Why can two brown-eyed parents have a blue-eyed child?

lesson.say: Genes come in versions called alleles. You inherit one allele from each parent. The genotype is the alleles you have. The phenotype is the trait you see.
lesson.html: Allele→Genotype: Bb→Phenotype: brown eyes

lesson.say: A dominant allele shows even if there is only one copy. A recessive allele only shows if there are two copies. Capital letter for dominant, small letter for recessive.
lesson.html:
BB: brown→Bb: brown→bb: blue

Homozygous: two the same. Heterozygous: two different.

lesson.say: A Punnett square shows possible offspring. If two Bb parents have children, there is a one in four chance of bb.
lesson.html:
B   b

B  BB Bb

b  Bb  bb

Ratio: 3 brown : 1 blue.

example.q: A Tt plant (tall) is crossed with a tt plant (short). What fraction of offspring will be short?
steps: Tt gives T or t. tt gives t only.
Offspring: Tt, Tt, tt, tt.
Half are tt, so 1/2 are short.

questions.q: What is a phenotype?
questions.explain: The phenotype is the observable trait.

questions.q: Which genotype is homozygous recessive?
questions.explain: aa is homozygous recessive.

questions.q: Two Bb parents. What is the chance of a bb child?
questions.explain: 1/4 chance of bb.

questions.q: Bb has brown eyes. What does this tell you?
questions.explain: Only one B is needed, so brown is dominant.

questions.q: Crossing AA with aa gives offspring that are all …
hints: AA gives A. aa gives a.
Every child gets one of each.
questions.explain: All offspring are Aa.

units.parent: Your child used Punnett squares to predict inherited traits.
units.teacher: Shows using genetic terminology, distinguishing dominance, and solving monohybrid crosses with Punnett squares.
units.done: Use a Punnett square to predict the chance of each genotype and phenotype.

units.subject: Life Sciences
units.title: Evolution by natural selection
units.caps: CAPS Grade 12 Life Sciences, Term 2: Evolution by natural selection (variation; Darwin's theory; artificial selection; speciation; evidence for evolution; human evolution and the Cradle of Humankind)
units.intention: Today I am learning how natural selection causes species to change over time.
units.prompt: How does antibiotic resistance show natural selection?

lesson.say: Individuals in a population vary. Some variation is inherited, coming from mutations and sexual reproduction.
lesson.html:
🐞🐞🐞

Without variation, selection cannot happen.

lesson.say: More offspring are born than can survive. Individuals with helpful traits survive and reproduce more. They pass these traits on. Over many generations, the population changes.
lesson.html:
Variation→Competition→Survival of the fittest→Inheritance→Change over time

Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace described this in the 1850s.

lesson.say: Evidence comes from fossils, comparing anatomy, and DNA. South Africa's Cradle of Humankind is a World Heritage Site. It has important hominin fossils, such as Mrs Ples and Little Foot.
lesson.html:
Fossils→Anatomy→DNA

The Cradle of Humankind is near Johannesburg.

example.q: Why do some bacteria survive antibiotics?
steps: Some bacteria have a mutation that gives resistance.
The antibiotic kills the others; the resistant ones survive and multiply.
Over time, the population becomes resistant. This is natural selection.

questions.q: What is needed for natural selection to happen?
hints: Some traits help more than others.
questions.explain: Variation is essential.

questions.q: Who proposed the theory of natural selection?
options: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace
questions.explain: Darwin and Wallace proposed it.

questions.q: What is artificial selection?
questions.explain: Humans choose which individuals reproduce.

questions.q: Where is the Cradle of Humankind?
questions.explain: It is near Johannesburg.

questions.q: Put natural selection in order.
questions.explain: Variation, competition, survival and reproduction, more common traits.

units.parent: Your child learned how natural selection works and the evidence for evolution, including South Africa's Cradle of Humankind.
units.teacher: Shows explaining natural selection, distinguishing artificial selection and identifying lines of evidence.
units.done: Natural selection favours helpful traits, changing populations over many generations.

units.subject: Life Orientation
units.title: Exam writing strategies
units.caps: CAPS Grade 12 Life Orientation: Study skills (exam writing skills; time management; managing exam stress)
units.intention: Today I am planning how to prepare for and write final exams.
units.prompt: Which strategy will help you most this exam season?

lesson.say: Work backwards from your exam dates. Give more time to harder subjects. Plan short sessions with breaks, and include rest days.
lesson.html:
Exam dates→Topics→Daily plan→Rest

Use past papers: they show question styles and timing.

lesson.say: Read the whole paper first. Plan your time using the marks. Start with questions you know to build confidence. Answer what is asked, and check your work at the end.
lesson.html:
Read all→Plan time→Start strong→Check

About 1 minute per mark is a useful guide.

lesson.say: Sleep matters more than late-night cramming. Eat regularly, drink water, move every day and take breaks. If you feel overwhelmed, talk to someone.
lesson.html: Sleep→Eat→Move→Breaks→Talk

example.q: A paper is 150 marks in 3 hours. How much time for a 30-mark question?
steps: 3 hours = 180 minutes for 150 marks.
About 1,2 minutes per mark.
30 marks ≈ 36 minutes.

questions.q: Why use past papers?
options: To practise question styles and timing
questions.explain: They help you practise style and timing.

questions.q: What should you do first in an exam?
options: Write your answers quickly without reading
questions.explain: Reading the whole paper helps you plan.

questions.q: Which is better the night before an exam?
hints: The brain consolidates memory in sleep.
questions.explain: Sleep helps memory and focus.

questions.q: A 100-mark paper lasts 2 hours. About how many minutes for a 25-mark section?
questions.explain: About 30 minutes.

questions.q: Why start with questions you know?
options: To build confidence and secure marks
questions.explain: It builds confidence and secures marks.

units.parent: Your child planned exam preparation and strategies for writing exams. Support with a quiet space and regular sleep.
units.teacher: Shows planning a study timetable, exam time management and self-care strategies.
units.done: Plan your study, manage time in the exam, and look after yourself.

units.subject: Life Orientation
units.title: Life after school
units.caps: CAPS Grade 12 Life Orientation: Careers and career choices (reasons for unemployment; innovative solutions; entrepreneurship; coping with change and the transition after school)
units.intention: Today I am planning for life after school, including if things do not go to plan.
units.prompt: What is your plan A, and what is your plan B?

lesson.say: After school you might study, work, do a learnership, volunteer, or start a business. Many people combine paths, and plans often change.
lesson.html:
Study→Work→Learnership→Volunteer→Business

Have a plan A and a plan B.

lesson.say: Youth unemployment in South Africa is very high. While searching, keep building skills: volunteer, do free online courses, take short courses and network. Register on government youth employment platforms.
lesson.html:
Volunteer→Learn online→Network→Register

A gap is not wasted if you keep growing.

lesson.say: An entrepreneur spots a need and creates a business to meet it. Start small, test your idea with real customers, keep records, and learn from mistakes.
lesson.html:
Spot a need→Test small→Keep records→Learn

Many successful businesses started with very little money.

example.q: Lwando did not get into university this year. What could he do?
steps: Find out why: marks, late application, or space.
Plan B: apply to a TVET college, a learnership, or improve marks with a supplementary or rewrite.
Meanwhile: volunteer, do a free course, and reapply on time next year.

questions.q: What is a plan B?
options: A backup if plan A does not work
questions.explain: Plan B is your backup.

questions.q: Which is a good use of time while job hunting?
questions.explain: Volunteering and learning build skills and contacts.

questions.q: What does an entrepreneur do?
options: Starts a business to meet a need
questions.explain: Entrepreneurs create businesses to meet needs.

questions.q: What is networking?
options: Building relationships that can lead to opportunities
questions.explain: Networking means building helpful connections.

questions.q: Why test a business idea small first?
options: To learn cheaply before investing more
questions.explain: Testing small reduces risk and teaches you quickly.

reflect.q: What will your next step be?

units.parent: Your child planned for life after school, including backup plans and entrepreneurship.
units.teacher: Shows awareness of post-school pathways, strategies for unemployment, and entrepreneurial thinking.
units.done: Have a plan A and a plan B, keep building skills, and consider starting something.

units.subject: Life Orientation
units.title: Responsible citizenship
units.topic: Democracy and human rights: voting and participation
units.caps: CAPS Grade 12 Life Orientation: Democracy and human rights (responsible citizenship; participation in civic life; voting; the role of the IEC)
units.intention: Today I am learning how to take part in democracy as an adult citizen.
units.prompt: Why might some young people not vote, and what could change that?

lesson.say: South African citizens can register to vote from age 16 and vote from age 18. The Electoral Commission of South Africa, the IEC, runs elections and keeps them free and fair.
lesson.html:
Register from 16→Vote from 18→IEC

You need your ID to register and vote.

lesson.say: Citizens also take part through ward committees, public participation in municipal plans, petitions, peaceful protest, and community organisations.
lesson.html:
Ward committees→Municipal plans→Petitions→Peaceful protest

Your ward councillor represents your area in the municipality.

lesson.say: Responsible citizens obey the law, pay taxes when they earn, respect others' rights, and stay informed.
lesson.html: Obey the law→Pay taxes→Respect rights→Stay informed

example.q: Thabo, 18, is unhappy that his street has no lights. What can he do?
steps: Contact his ward councillor and report it to the municipality.
Attend a ward committee meeting or comment on the municipal plan.
Make sure he is registered so he can vote in the next local election.

questions.q: From what age can you vote in South Africa?
questions.explain: You can vote from 18.

questions.q: Who runs elections in South Africa?
questions.explain: The Electoral Commission (IEC) runs elections.

questions.q: Who represents your area in the municipality?
questions.explain: Your ward councillor represents your ward.

questions.q: Which is a peaceful way to participate?
questions.explain: A petition is a peaceful form of participation.

questions.q: Which is a citizen's responsibility?
questions.explain: Respecting others' rights is a key responsibility.

units.parent: Your child learned how citizens take part in democracy, including registering to vote.
units.teacher: Shows knowledge of voting rights, the IEC, local government participation and civic responsibilities.
units.done: Register, vote, and take part in your community's decisions.

units.subject: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
units.title: The binomial theorem
units.caps: IB Diploma Programme Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches (SL/HL): Topic 1, number and algebra (binomial theorem; Pascal's triangle; ⁿCᵣ)
units.intention: Today I am expanding powers of brackets with the binomial theorem.
units.prompt: What patterns can you see in Pascal's triangle?

lesson.say: Each number in Pascal's triangle is the sum of the two above it. The rows give the coefficients for expanding a plus b to a power.
The binomial theorem expands a plus b to the n. It is the sum of n choose r, times a to the n minus r, times b to the r.
lesson.html: (a + b)ⁿ = Σ ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ

lesson.say: The general term is n choose r, a to the n minus r, b to the r. For example, find the x squared term in x plus 2 to the 5. Use r equals 3. That gives 10 times x squared times 8, which is 80 x squared.
lesson.html: ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ → ⁵C₃ x² 2³ = 80x²

lesson.say: Theory of Knowledge link: Pascal's triangle was known in China, Persia and India centuries before Pascal. What does this suggest about who gets credit for knowledge?
lesson.html: TOK link: Pascal's triangle was known in China, Persia and India centuries before Pascal. What does this suggest about who gets credit for knowledge?

example.q: Expand (x + 1)³.
steps: Row 3 of Pascal's triangle: 1, 3, 3, 1.
x³ + 3x² + 3x + 1.

questions.q: What is ⁵C₂?
questions.explain: ⁵C₂ = 10.

questions.q: Which is row 4 of Pascal's triangle?
Find the coefficient of x² in (x + 2)⁴.
How many terms are in the expansion of (a + b)⁷?
hints: Always one more than the power.
questions.explain: (a + b)ⁿ has n + 1 terms.

questions.q: What is the constant term in (x + 3)²?
questions.explain: x² + 6x + 9; the constant term is 9.

units.parent: Your child used the binomial theorem to expand powers of brackets.
units.teacher: Shows using Pascal's triangle and ⁿCᵣ, applying the binomial theorem and finding specific terms.
units.done: Use ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ; the coefficients come from Pascal's triangle.

units.subject: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
units.title: The chi-squared test
units.caps: IB Diploma Programme Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation (SL/HL): Topic 4, statistics (χ² test for independence; hypotheses; p-values; degrees of freedom)
units.intention: Today I am testing whether two variables are independent.
units.prompt: Does gender affect which sport people prefer? How could you test it?

lesson.say: The null hypothesis says the variables are independent. The alternative says they are not. We test at a significance level, often 5 percent.
lesson.html: H₀: independent · H₁: not independent · level 5%

lesson.say: For each cell, the expected frequency is row total times column total, divided by the grand total. The chi-squared statistic measures how far observed values are from expected.
lesson.html: Expected = (row total × column total) ÷ grand total

lesson.say: If the p-value is less than the significance level, reject the null hypothesis. Degrees of freedom are rows minus 1, times columns minus 1.
lesson.html: p < 0.05 → reject H₀ · df = (r − 1)(c − 1)

lesson.say: Theory of Knowledge link: A 5% significance level means we will sometimes be wrong. How much uncertainty is acceptable in knowledge claims?
lesson.html: TOK link: A 5% significance level means we will sometimes be wrong. How much uncertainty is acceptable in knowledge claims?

example.q: A 2 × 3 table gives p = 0.02 at the 5% level. What do you conclude?
steps: Reject H₀.
There is evidence that the variables are not independent.

questions.q: What does H₀ state in a χ² test for independence?
questions.explain: H₀: the variables are independent.

questions.q: Row total 40, column total 50, grand total 200. Find the expected frequency.
How many degrees of freedom for a 3 × 4 table?
At the 5% level, p = 0.12. What do you do?
questions.explain: 0.12 > 0.05, so there isn't enough evidence to reject H₀.

questions.q: Why should expected frequencies not be too small?
hints: Expected values should usually be at least 5.
questions.explain: Small expected frequencies make the test unreliable.

units.parent: Your child learnt to test whether two things are linked, using a statistical test.
units.teacher: Shows stating hypotheses, calculating expected frequencies and degrees of freedom, and drawing conclusions from p-values.
units.done: State H₀, compare p with the level, and conclude in context.

units.subject: Language A: Language and Literature
units.title: Exploring a global issue
units.caps: IB Diploma Programme Language A: Language and Literature (SL/HL): individual oral (exploring a global issue through a literary and a non-literary text)
units.intention: Today I am planning how two texts explore a global issue.
units.prompt: Which global issue matters most to you?

lesson.say: In the individual oral, you explore one global issue. You look at how it is presented in one literary text and one non-literary text. You discuss their content and their form.
lesson.html: Global issue→Literary text→Non-literary text

lesson.say: A global issue is significant and transnational, which means it crosses borders. It is felt in everyday life. Examples are access to education, gender roles and the impact of technology.
lesson.html: Significant→Transnational→Everyday impact

lesson.say: Choose a short extract from each text. Analyse how the authors' choices present the issue, and compare the two texts, rather than just retelling them.
lesson.html: Content and form · compare, don't retell

lesson.say: Theory of Knowledge link: Can a work of fiction give us knowledge about real global issues?
lesson.html: TOK link: Can a work of fiction give us knowledge about real global issues?

example.q: How might a poem and the texting-and-driving poster explore 'the impact of technology'?
steps: Issue: technology's effect on attention and safety.
The poster uses an empty desk to show the cost of distraction.
A poem might use imagery of screens and absence; comparing their methods shows two angles on one issue.

questions.q: How many texts does the individual oral use?
questions.explain: One literary and one non-literary text.

questions.q: Which is a suitable global issue?
questions.explain: Access to education is significant and transnational.

questions.q: What should the oral focus on?
options: How each text's content and form present the issue
questions.explain: Analyse how the texts present the issue.

questions.q: Why choose short extracts?
questions.explain: Short extracts allow close analysis within the time.

questions.q: Which sentence compares the texts?
options: While the poster shocks with a single image, the poem builds unease slowly through repetition.
questions.explain: It compares how each text presents the issue.

units.parent: Your child planned how to explore a global issue through two different texts.
units.teacher: Individual oral: shows selecting a global issue and planning comparative analysis of content and form across text types.
units.done: One global issue, two texts: compare how each presents it.

units.subject: Chemistry
units.title: Equilibrium and Le Chatelier's principle
units.caps: IB Diploma Programme Chemistry (SL/HL): dynamic equilibrium; Le Chatelier's principle; effect of conditions on equilibrium position
units.intention: Today I am predicting how equilibria respond to change.
units.prompt: Why does a fizzy drink go flat when you open it?

lesson.say: In a closed system, a reversible reaction reaches dynamic equilibrium. The forward and reverse reactions keep going at equal rates. So the concentrations stay constant.
lesson.html: Rate forward = rate reverse · concentrations constant

lesson.say: If conditions change, the equilibrium shifts to oppose the change. Adding a reactant shifts it to the right. Increasing pressure shifts it towards fewer gas molecules.
lesson.html: Add reactant: shift right→More pressure: fewer gas moles→Catalyst: no shift

lesson.say: Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction. A catalyst speeds up both directions equally, so it doesn't change the position of equilibrium.
lesson.html: Heat → favours endothermic direction

lesson.say: Theory of Knowledge link: Le Chatelier's principle predicts but doesn't explain. Is a useful rule the same as understanding?
lesson.html: TOK link: Le Chatelier's principle predicts but doesn't explain. Is a useful rule the same as understanding?

example.q: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (exothermic). What happens to the yield of ammonia if pressure increases?
steps: Left side: 4 gas moles; right side: 2.
Higher pressure favours fewer gas moles.
The equilibrium shifts right, increasing the yield of ammonia.

questions.q: At dynamic equilibrium…
options: forward and reverse rates are equal
questions.explain: Both reactions continue at equal rates.

questions.q: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ is exothermic. Raising the temperature…
options: shifts equilibrium left and lowers the yield
questions.explain: Higher temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction.

questions.q: What effect does a catalyst have on the position of equilibrium?
questions.explain: A catalyst speeds both directions equally.

questions.q: More H₂ is added to N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. What happens?
hints: It uses up the extra H₂.
questions.explain: The system shifts right to use up the added reactant.

questions.q: Why does a fizzy drink go flat when opened?
options: Lower pressure shifts CO₂ out of solution
questions.explain: Releasing pressure shifts the equilibrium so CO₂ leaves the solution.

units.parent: Your child predicted how chemical equilibria respond to changes in conditions.
units.teacher: Shows describing dynamic equilibrium and applying Le Chatelier's principle to concentration, pressure, temperature and catalysts.
units.done: The equilibrium shifts to oppose any change; a catalyst doesn't shift it.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Momentum and impulse
units.caps: IB Diploma Programme Physics (SL/HL): momentum and impulse; conservation of linear momentum; collisions
units.intention: Today I am using conservation of momentum in collisions.
units.prompt: Why do airbags reduce injuries?

lesson.say: Momentum is mass times velocity, measured in kilogram metres per second. It is a vector, so direction matters.
lesson.html: p = mv

lesson.say: In an isolated system, total momentum before a collision equals total momentum after.
lesson.html: Σp before = Σp after

lesson.say: Impulse is force times time, and it equals the change in momentum. Airbags increase the time of impact, so the force on the passenger is smaller.
lesson.html: FΔt = Δp · longer Δt → smaller F

lesson.say: Theory of Knowledge link: Conservation laws are assumed to hold everywhere in the universe. On what basis can we make such a universal claim?
lesson.html: TOK link: Conservation laws are assumed to hold everywhere in the universe. On what basis can we make such a universal claim?

example.q: A 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg trolley, and they stick together. Find their velocity.
steps: Momentum before: 2 × 3 + 1 × 0 = 6 kg m/s.
After: (2 + 1)v = 6.
v = 2 m/s.

questions.q: Find the momentum of a 5 kg ball moving at 4 m/s, in kg m/s.
A 3 kg cart at 4 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg cart, and they stick together. Find their speed, in m/s.
A force of 10 N acts for 3 s. What is the impulse, in N s?
Why do airbags reduce injury?
options: They increase the impact time, reducing the force
questions.explain: A longer stopping time means a smaller force for the same change in momentum.

questions.q: Why is momentum a vector?
options: It depends on velocity, which has direction
questions.explain: Momentum has the direction of the velocity.

units.parent: Your child used momentum to analyse collisions and explain car safety features.
units.teacher: Shows calculating momentum and impulse and applying conservation of momentum to collisions.
units.done: Total momentum is conserved; impulse = FΔt = change in momentum.

units.subject: Theory of Knowledge
units.title: Building a TOK essay argument
units.caps: IB Diploma Programme Theory of Knowledge: the TOK essay (claims, counterclaims and real-life examples across two areas of knowledge)
units.intention: Today I am building claims and counterclaims for a TOK essay.
units.prompt: Can you think of something experts were once certain about that turned out to be wrong?

lesson.say: The TOK essay answers one of six prescribed titles, in up to 1 600 words, usually exploring two areas of knowledge.
lesson.html: Up to 1 600 words · a prescribed title · two areas of knowledge

lesson.say: Each claim is supported by a specific real-life example and then tested with a counterclaim. This shows you see more than one side.
lesson.html: Claim→Example→Counterclaim→Example→Evaluation

lesson.say: Use specific, real examples, not hypothetical ones. For instance, the shift from Newton's to Einstein's physics shows that even very successful scientific knowledge can be revised.
lesson.html: Specific and real: Newton → Einstein

example.q: Title idea: 'Is certainty possible in the natural sciences?' Give a claim and a counterclaim.
steps: Claim: scientific knowledge is provisional; Newton's laws were revised by Einstein.
Counterclaim: some findings, such as the Earth orbiting the Sun, are so well supported they are effectively certain.
Evaluation: science aims at reliability rather than absolute certainty.

questions.q: What is the maximum length of the TOK essay, in words?
questions.explain: The TOK essay is up to 1 600 words.

questions.q: What is a counterclaim?
options: A point that challenges your claim
questions.explain: A counterclaim tests your claim from another angle.

questions.q: Which is the best example?
options: The revision of Newton's physics by Einstein's relativity
questions.explain: It is a real, specific example from the history of science.

questions.q: What should follow a claim and counterclaim?
questions.explain: Evaluation shows your judgement.

questions.q: Why explore two areas of knowledge?
options: To compare how knowledge works in different areas
questions.explain: Comparing areas reveals differences in how knowledge is made.

units.parent: Your child built claims and counterclaims for a Theory of Knowledge essay.
units.teacher: TOK essay: shows constructing claims and counterclaims supported by specific real-life examples and evaluating them across areas of knowledge.
units.done: Claim, example, counterclaim, example, then evaluate.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Calculus in context: optimisation
units.caps: IEB Mathematics (CAPS content, IEB assessment): Grade 12 differential calculus: optimisation in unfamiliar contexts
units.intention: Today I am using calculus to find the best possible value.
units.prompt: How would a farmer get the biggest field from a fixed amount of fencing?

lesson.say: Optimisation means finding a maximum or minimum, such as the largest area or the lowest cost. At a maximum or minimum, the derivative is zero.
lesson.html: At a max or min: f′(x) = 0

lesson.say: A farmer has 40 metres of fencing for a rectangle against a wall. The wall is one side, so only three sides need fencing. Let the two short sides be x. Then the long side is 40 minus 2x. The area is x times 40 minus 2x.
The derivative is 40 minus 4x. Set it to zero: x equals 10. The long side is 20, so the largest area is 200 square metres.

example.q: Check that x = 10 gives a maximum.
steps: A negative second derivative means the graph is concave down.
So x = 10 gives a maximum.

questions.q: At a maximum or minimum, what is the derivative?
questions.explain: The gradient is zero at a turning point.

questions.q: If A = 40x − 2x², what is A′?
Solve 40 − 4x = 0.
With x = 10, the area is 10 × (40 − 20). What is it, in m²?
Why must 0 < x < 20 here?
options: Both sides must have positive length
Fences are always shorter than 20 m
questions.explain: Both x and 40 − 2x must be positive.

units.parent: Your child used calculus to find the biggest possible area for a fixed amount of fencing.
units.teacher: Shows formulating a function from context, using f′(x) = 0 to optimise, verifying the nature of the turning point and applying domain restrictions.
units.done: Write the function, set the derivative to zero, solve, and check.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Proof and counterexample
units.caps: IEB Mathematics (CAPS content, IEB assessment): Grade 12 reasoning: proving general statements and disproving with counterexamples
units.intention: Today I am proving statements, or disproving them with one example.
units.prompt: How many examples does it take to prove something is always true?

lesson.say: To prove a statement is always true, use algebra that covers every case. Checking a few examples is not a proof.
lesson.html: Examples suggest. Algebra proves.

lesson.say: Prove that the sum of two consecutive integers is odd. Let them be n and n plus 1. Their sum is 2n plus 1. 2n is even, so 2n plus 1 is odd, for every integer n.
lesson.html: n + (n + 1) = 2n + 1 → always odd

lesson.say: To disprove a statement, one counterexample is enough. 'All prime numbers are odd' is false, because 2 is prime and even.
lesson.html: One counterexample disproves a general claim.

example.q: Prove that the product of two even numbers is a multiple of 4.
steps: Let the numbers be 2a and 2b.
Product: 2a × 2b = 4ab.
4ab is a multiple of 4 for all integers a and b.

questions.q: What disproves 'All prime numbers are odd'?
hints: Find a prime that is even.
questions.explain: 2 is prime and even.

questions.q: How do we write a general even number in algebra?
questions.explain: 2n is even for every integer n.

questions.q: Why doesn't checking 10 examples prove a statement?
options: The next case might not work
questions.explain: Examples can't cover every case.

questions.q: 'n² + n + 41 is always prime.' Which value of n is a counterexample?
questions.explain: When n = 40, the value is 1 681 = 41², which isn't prime.

questions.q: n + (n + 1) = 2n + 1. Why does this prove the sum is odd?
options: 2n is even, and adding 1 makes it odd for every n
questions.explain: An even number plus 1 is always odd.

options: Explaining why a proof is general

units.parent: Your child proved general statements with algebra and disproved others with counterexamples.
units.teacher: Shows constructing algebraic proofs, recognising the limits of empirical checking and using counterexamples.
units.done: Prove with algebra for every case; disprove with one counterexample.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Responding to an unseen poem
units.caps: IEB English Home Language (CAPS content, IEB assessment): Grade 12 unseen poetry: planning and writing a focused critical response
units.intention: Today I am planning a critical response to a poem I haven't seen before.
units.prompt: What do you do first when you read a new poem?
units.passage:
Inheritance (a 2to.iQ poem)

My grandmother's hands were maps:
rivers of blue under paper skin,
a scar where the paraffin stove
once argued with her.

She never wrote a letter in her life,
yet every recipe I know
is written in the margins of her palms,
and I am still learning to read them.

lesson.say: Read the source, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
Inheritance (a 2to.iQ poem)

My grandmother's hands were maps:
rivers of blue under paper skin,
a scar where the paraffin stove
once argued with her.

She never wrote a letter in her life,
yet every recipe I know
is written in the margins of her palms,
and I am still learning to read them.

lesson.say: Read once for the overall meaning, then again with the question in mind. Underline images, word choices and shifts in tone.
lesson.html: Overall meaning→Re-read for the question→Mark key words

lesson.say: Answer the question in one sentence, and then prove it. For example: the poem shows the grandmother's body as a record of knowledge passed on without writing.
lesson.html: Thesis: an answer you will prove

lesson.say: Look for where the poem turns. Here the second stanza moves from describing her hands to what the speaker inherited. Shifts like this are often the key to meaning.
lesson.html: Find the turn.

example.q: Write a topic sentence about the first stanza.
steps: Focus: the hands as a record of hardship.
Evidence: 'a scar where the paraffin stove once argued with her'.
'The first stanza presents her hands as a record of a hard life, with the personified stove suggesting daily struggle.'

questions.q: What should you do on a second reading?
options: Re-read with the question in mind and mark key words
questions.explain: A focused second reading targets what the question asks.

questions.q: What technique is 'the paraffin stove once argued with her'?
questions.explain: The stove is given a human action.

questions.q: Where does the poem turn?
options: At the start of the second stanza
questions.explain: The second stanza shifts to the speaker's inheritance.

questions.q: Which is the best thesis?
options: The poem presents the grandmother's hands as a record of knowledge passed on without writing.
questions.explain: It is a focused interpretation that can be proved.

questions.q: What does 'She never wrote a letter in her life' add?
options: A contrast with the 'writing' in her palms
A fact about the post office
questions.explain: It contrasts formal writing with knowledge held in her hands.

units.parent: Your child planned a critical response to an unseen poem.
units.teacher: Shows approaching unseen poetry systematically, formulating a focused thesis and analysing imagery and structural shifts.
units.done: Read twice, find the turn, write a thesis, then prove it.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Writing a report from sources
units.caps: IEB English Home Language (CAPS content, IEB assessment): Grade 12 transactional writing: synthesising sources into a formal report
units.intention: Today I am writing a formal report using information from sources.
units.prompt: Who reads reports, and what do they need from them?

lesson.say: A report informs a decision-maker. It is formal, clear and organised under headings, with a recommendation at the end.
lesson.html: Introduction→Findings→Recommendation

lesson.say: Combine information from several sources, in your own words. Group related points together instead of summarising each source separately.
lesson.html: Group by theme, not by source.

lesson.say: Use the third person, avoid slang and contractions, and keep opinions for the recommendation, supported by the findings.
lesson.html: Formal: third person, no slang, no contractions.

example.q: Turn a source note into a formal finding: 'loads of kids walk like 5km in the dark'.
steps: Remove slang and vague words.
Use precise, third-person language.
'A significant number of learners walk more than five kilometres to school before sunrise.'

questions.q: Who is a report usually written for?
options: Someone who must make a decision
questions.explain: Reports inform decision-makers.

questions.q: How should information from several sources be organised?
questions.explain: Grouping by theme shows synthesis.

questions.q: Which sentence suits a formal report?
options: Learner attendance decreased by 12% during winter.
Loads of kids didn't pitch in winter.
questions.explain: It is formal, precise and in the third person.

questions.q: Where does the writer's recommendation belong?
options: At the end, supported by the findings
questions.explain: The recommendation follows from the findings.

questions.q: Which is a contraction to avoid in formal writing?
questions.explain: Write 'do not' instead of 'don't'.

units.parent: Your child practised writing a formal report from several sources.
units.teacher: Shows synthesising information across sources, organising a formal report and maintaining an appropriate register.
units.done: Inform the decision-maker: group by theme, stay formal, end with a recommendation.

units.subject: Life Sciences
units.title: Evidence for evolution: resistance
units.caps: IEB Life Sciences (CAPS content, IEB assessment): Grade 12 evolution by natural selection: interpreting data on antibiotic resistance
units.intention: Today I am using data to explain natural selection.
units.prompt: Why must you finish a course of antibiotics?

lesson.say: Individuals in a population vary. Some variations help survival. Those individuals survive, reproduce and pass on the helpful alleles, so the population changes over generations.
lesson.html: Variation→Selection→Survival and reproduction→Change over generations

lesson.say: In a made-up hospital study, 5 percent of a bacterial population was resistant to an antibiotic in year 1. After years of heavy antibiotic use, 60 percent was resistant by year 6.
lesson.html: Resistant bacteria: year 1 = 5% → year 6 = 60%

lesson.say: The antibiotic killed non-resistant bacteria. Resistant ones survived and reproduced, so the proportion of resistant bacteria increased.
lesson.html: The antibiotic is the selecting agent.

example.q: Use the data to explain the increase in resistance.
steps: Resistance rose from 5% to 60% over 6 years.
The antibiotic killed non-resistant bacteria, while resistant ones survived.
Survivors reproduced and passed on resistance, so it became more common.

questions.q: Resistance rose from 5% to 60%. By how many percentage points did it rise?
questions.explain: 60 − 5 = 55 percentage points.

questions.q: What is the selecting agent in this example?
questions.explain: The antibiotic selects against non-resistant bacteria.

questions.q: Where did the resistance come from?
options: Variation already present in the population
The antibiotic created it on purpose
questions.explain: Some bacteria were already resistant; the antibiotic didn't create it.

questions.q: Why does not finishing a course of antibiotics help resistance spread?
options: The more resistant bacteria may survive and multiply
questions.explain: Stopping early can leave the most resistant bacteria to multiply.

questions.q: Which statement uses the data correctly?
options: Resistance increased from 5% to 60% over six years of heavy antibiotic use.
questions.explain: It reports the data accurately without exaggerating.

options: The four steps of natural selection

units.parent: Your child used data to explain how bacteria become resistant to antibiotics.
units.teacher: Shows explaining natural selection with reference to data, identifying the selecting agent and avoiding Lamarckian misconceptions.
units.done: Variation, selection, survival and reproduction: support each step with data.

units.subject: Life Sciences
units.title: Genetics and ethics
units.caps: IEB Life Sciences (CAPS content, IEB assessment): Grade 12 genetics: evaluating the benefits and concerns of genetic technologies
units.intention: Today I am weighing up the benefits and concerns of genetic technology.
units.prompt: Should everyone know their genetic risks?

lesson.say: Genetic technologies include genetically modified crops, genetic testing and DNA profiling. Each brings benefits and raises concerns.
lesson.html: GM crops→Genetic testing→DNA profiling

lesson.say: GM maize can resist pests, so farmers need less pesticide. But some people worry about the cost of seed for small farmers. They also worry about effects on biodiversity.
lesson.html: Benefit: fewer pests, less spraying · Concern: seed costs, biodiversity

lesson.say: Ethics asks what is right. Who owns genetic information? Should insurers see it? A balanced answer presents both sides, then reaches a justified view.
lesson.html: Present both sides, then a justified view.

example.q: Give one benefit and one concern of genetic testing for disease risk.
steps: Benefit: people can take early action, such as screening or lifestyle changes.
Concern: the information could be misused, for example by insurers or employers.
A balanced answer weighs both and suggests protections, such as privacy laws.

questions.q: What is one benefit of pest-resistant GM maize?
options: It is always cheaper for every farmer
It removes all pests for ever
questions.explain: Pest resistance can reduce pesticide use.

questions.q: What is one concern about GM seed for small farmers?
options: The cost of buying patented seed each season
questions.explain: Patented seed can be expensive to buy every season.

questions.q: Which is an ethical question about genetic testing?
options: Should insurers be allowed to see the results?
How long is a DNA molecule?
How many genes do humans have?
questions.explain: It asks what is right, not what is true.

questions.q: DNA profiling is used to…
options: identify individuals, for example in forensic cases
questions.explain: DNA profiling identifies people from their DNA.

questions.q: What makes an ethics answer strong?
options: Presenting both sides and reaching a justified view
questions.explain: Strong answers weigh both sides and justify a view.

units.parent: Your child weighed up the benefits and concerns of genetic technologies.
units.teacher: Shows describing genetic technologies, evaluating benefits and concerns, and constructing balanced, justified ethical arguments.
units.done: Present the benefits and the concerns, then reach a justified view.

units.subject: Advanced Programme Mathematics
units.title: Integration and area
units.caps: IEB Advanced Programme Mathematics: Module 1, Calculus (antiderivatives and definite integrals; area under a curve)
units.intention: Today I am integrating to find the area under a curve.
units.prompt: How could you find the area of a shape with a curved edge?

lesson.say: Integration reverses differentiation. The integral of x to the n is x to the n plus 1, over n plus 1, plus a constant c.
lesson.html: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹ ÷ (n + 1) + c, for n ≠ −1

lesson.say: A definite integral from a to b gives a number. First find the antiderivative. Then subtract its value at a from its value at b.
lesson.html: ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a)

lesson.say: For a curve above the x-axis, the definite integral gives the area between the curve and the axis. The area under y equals x squared from 0 to 3 is 9.
lesson.html: ∫ from 0 to 3 of x² dx = [x³ ÷ 3] from 0 to 3 = 9

example.q: Find ∫ from 1 to 2 of 2x dx.
steps: The antiderivative of 2x is x².

questions.q: What is ∫ x³ dx?
questions.explain: ∫ x³ dx = x⁴ ÷ 4 + c.

questions.q: Why add + c to an indefinite integral?
options: Constants vanish when you differentiate, so any constant is possible
questions.explain: Any constant differentiates to 0, so it must be included.

questions.q: Find ∫ from 0 to 2 of 3x² dx.
questions.explain: [x³] from 0 to 2 = 8.

questions.q: Find the area under y = 4 from x = 0 to x = 5.
questions.explain: ∫ from 0 to 5 of 4 dx = 20.

questions.q: Integration is the reverse of…
questions.explain: Integration reverses differentiation.

units.parent: Your child integrated functions and used integration to find areas.
units.teacher: Shows finding antiderivatives of power functions, evaluating definite integrals and interpreting them as area.
units.done: Raise the power, divide by it, then evaluate F(b) − F(a).

units.subject: Advanced Programme Mathematics
units.title: The normal distribution
units.caps: IEB Advanced Programme Mathematics: Module 2, Statistics (the normal distribution and z-scores)
units.intention: Today I am using the normal distribution and z-scores.
units.prompt: Why are most people close to average height?

lesson.say: Many measurements, like heights, follow a normal distribution: a symmetrical bell-shaped curve centred on the mean.
lesson.html: Symmetrical about the mean.

lesson.say: About 68 percent of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean, about 95 percent within 2, and about 99.7 percent within 3.
lesson.html: ±1σ: 68%→±2σ: 95%→±3σ: 99.7%

lesson.say: A z-score tells you how many standard deviations a value is from the mean. The formula is: z equals x minus the mean, divided by the standard deviation.

example.q: Test marks have a mean of 60 and a standard deviation of 10. Find the z-score of a mark of 75.
steps: = 1.5: the mark is 1.5 standard deviations above the mean.

questions.q: Mean 60, standard deviation 10. Find the z-score of 80.
About what percentage of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean?
questions.explain: About 68% lie within ±1σ.

questions.q: What does a z-score of −1 mean?
options: The value is 1 standard deviation below the mean
questions.explain: z = −1 is one standard deviation below the mean.

questions.q: Heights: mean 160 cm, σ = 8 cm. About 95% of heights lie between 144 cm and what height, in cm?
What shape is a normal distribution?
hints: Most values are near the middle.
questions.explain: It is a symmetrical bell-shaped curve.

units.parent: Your child used the normal distribution and z-scores to describe data.
units.teacher: Shows applying the empirical rule, calculating and interpreting z-scores in context.
units.done: Bell-shaped and symmetrical: 68, 95, 99.7, and z = (x − μ) ÷ σ.
